body:
Hi @scott91e1 I'll be reviewing this according to the license inclusion principles.
I've just begun to look at it so please don't mind if it takes me a day or so to type it out
Thanks for the heads up.  This is my first license submission so if there are any issues or you have any suggestions to improve/tighten the language I would be happy to hear them.  Scott.

I've reviewed the license and have checked the checkboxes next to each factor of the license inclusion principles that in my estimation match the license, and left empty checkboxes next to each factor that does not match.

## Definitive factors (3/3, 2 N/A):

- [x] The submitted license must not match another license already on the SPDX License List as per the SPDX matching guidelines.
**This is a unique license text.**
- [ ] All OSI-approved licenses will be included on the SPDX License List.
**Not applicable**
- [ ] Software licenses that apply only to executables and do not provide for the availability of the source code will not be included on the SPDX License List.
**Not applicable**
- [x] The license has identifiable and stable text; it is not in the midst of drafting.
**Submitter is the license steward, and I presume that upon submission to SPDX submitter has completed drafting the license.**
- [x] The license steward, if any, is committed to not modifying after addition to the list and to versioning new versions in the future.
**License is versioned. Presumably a future revision would have a new version number.**

## Other factors (roughly in order of importance) (2/5 factors):

- [ ] The license substantially complies with one of the following open source definitions (even if not submitted for approval or these organization have not considered the license):

    Open Source Definition (OSD) from the Open Source Initiative (OSI)
    Free Software Definition from the Free Software Foundation (FSF)
    Open Source Hardware Definition from the Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA)
    Open Definition from the Open Knowledge Foundation
    Free Cultural Works definition from Freedom Defined.org
**In my review I found the license doesn't meet open source or free software definitions.**
- [x] The license is structured to be generally usable by anyone. It is not specific to one project, consortium or corporation.
**It is written in a general manner.**
- [ ] The license has actual, substantial use such that it is likely to be encountered. Substantial use may be demonstrated via use in many projects, or in one or a few significant projects. For new licenses, there are definitive plans for the license to be used in one or a few significant projects.
**Submitter has not demonstrated substantial use, or definitive plans to be used in significant projects.**
- [ ] If the license does not substantively comply with one of the above open source definitions, then the license is primarily intended for free distribution of content (including, in the case of software, its source code) with limited restrictions, and meets other factors listed here.
**In my review I found the restrictions against free distribution of content to be wide-reaching. Restrictions against free distribution are the main feature of the license.**
- [x] The license steward supports or is at least aware of and does not oppose its submission to the SPDX License List.
**Submitter is the license steward.**

This license was discussed in the SPDX-legal biweekly meeting dated 27 May 2021.

# Conclusion

Without followups to address some of the Other Factors listed above, it is unlikely for this license to be considered for inclusion in the SPDX list. If you have a question about any of the above, feel free to submit them as replies to this Github issue.

Note: If a license is *not* accepted for inclusion on the SPDX License List, you can use the 'LicenseRef-[idstring]' tag to identify your license, as per [SPDX specification, section 6](https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/6-other-licensing-information-detected/)
Discussed on 2021-06-10 legal team call (as well as call 2 weeks ago), agreed not to add at this time based on analysis of the inclusion principles.

Thanks for this consideration of this new category of open source license.

I would like to understand, however, how the "SPDX: Hippocratic-2.1" was approved considering it includes "termination of this License for breach of the Human Rights Principles" and this is typically country-based and therefore would also be contrary to the "inclusion principles".

It seems that the "Programing-Unity-10.42" license is was rejected as it has concrete anti-discrimination provisions where "Hippocratic-2.1" is similar in spirit but is aspirational in implementation.

@scott91e1 Your reply is very helpful, as this is my first ever review and it helps me understand where I could apply more care in crafting the review. I'm sorry for not being more verbose in the review itself, as I'm still finding the right balance. @swinslow's remarks in #1098, copied here, also apply to your license application.

> For the "other factors", we look at them with a "totality of the factors" lens. Given that, based in particular on it not meeting factors 1 and 3, and the uncertainty around 4, I'm inclined to recommend that it should not be added to the License List at present. For licenses that don't meet one of the listed definitions (factor 1), we typically want to see greater evidence of broad use in the wild (factor 3). Some licenses such as Hippocratic-2.1 have been added on that basis, but in that case significantly greater usage was shown.

[Here is the link](https://github.com/search?q=hippocratic+license&type=commits) Hippocratic-2.1's submitter shared to demonstrate substantial use. They also gave 3-4 examples of use in the body of the submission itself.

I'd also like to alleviate your concerns about the implementation of the review process itself. Whether a license is "concrete" or "aspirational" isn't marked in the review process. Only the factors listed in the inclusion principles apply to my review.

Thanks for the additional information.  It's also my first license submission, so understanding the process and objectives of SPDX firsthand as a submitter is new to me.

Can the "LicenseRef-" prefix be used as the SPDX license identifier when submitting projects to PyPI.org?  I don't mind that the LGBTIQ+ license being considered an "unofficial license," but I would like to use it for my Python projects.

If this is not possible, perhaps a new prefix could be launched, "Nursery-" or similar for upcoming licenses that meet the bulk of the criteria sans adoption.

It seems to me there is a chicken-and-egg situation when launching new software licenses.

As pydigger.com seems to show, it seems PyPI allows any string in the license field: https://pydigger.com/licenses. I see a couple entries using LicenseRef-.

> I don't mind that the LGBTIQ+ license being considered an "unofficial license,"

I understand where this misconception comes from, but the SPDX license request process does not judge licenses "official" or "unofficial." SPDX automatically accepts OSI-approved licenses, which is the only "stamp of approval" criterion for license list inclusion. My evaluation of whether your license complies with the Open Source Definition would be overwritten if the OSI approves it.

You don't need any outside organization's stamp of approval to use a text as a license, however, and SPDX does not provide a qualitative opinion on license texts. SPDX reviewers only apply the criteria of other organizations.
